items.title: [fix][CB] Fix the blend-rate regression: all-or-nothing scatter + per-range applied dedup

labels.name: full
labels.description: Run comprehensive tests on this PR

items.body:
## What

Two fixes in `cb_retrieve_pre_computed`:

1. **All-or-nothing scatter.** Every match beyond the allocated slots → defer (noop success; nothing forwarded yet, the follow-up call scatters everything, locks stay held). Partially covered → `scatter_ran=False` (client degrades; a success here would blend unpopulated KV — the old gate had this hazard for a boundary-spanning match). The in-loop per-match drop is unreachable and raises.

2. **Per-range applied dedup.** The applied-range skip was keyed on a crc32 of the request's *whole* destination table. vLLM re-calls retrieve as the block table grows, so plain growth changed the key, the skip never matched, and the repeat re-read keys whose locks the first call had already released: `KEY_NOT_READABLE` → `scatter_ran=False` → the request degrades after its blend was already applied. Now the key is the destination blocks each range actually writes into; growth beyond an applied range no longer invalidates it, a reassigned destination still re-scatters.

## Why

The blend rate on MiniMax-M3 bench_quality was capped at 14.4 vs 18.0 historical: 7/23 warm requests hit a repeat retrieve and every one degraded (112 rank-degrades, 1576 failed re-reads). Fix 2 removes the false dedup misses that trigger the failing re-reads; fix 1 guarantees a request's applied/lock state is never partial, so a repeat is either a clean no-op or a clean failure.

items.title: [Fix][CB] Key the applied-range skip on the blocks each range actually writes
items.body:
`cb_retrieve_pre_computed` keeps an applied-range set so vLLM's repeat call
(partial- then full-block alloc) skips ranges it already scattered. That set was
keyed on `crc32` of the **entire** destination block table — which also changes when
the allocation merely **grows**, and growth is precisely why the repeat call happens.
So the guard mistook *"more blocks allocated"* for *"my destination moved"*, never
matched, and every repeat re-scattered work already done.

Measured on minimax_m3 `bench_quality`: **1** `already_applied` hit against **3,328**
failed reads.

## The change

The key now carries the destination blocks **that range** actually writes into. A tuple
of block ids is hashable, so no fingerprint is needed at all — which drops the `crc32`
and its (remote) collision risk, and lets the `zlib` import go:

```python
def _dest(r: "CBMatchResult") -> tuple:
    out: list[int] = []
    try:
        for kg in _staged_kgs:
            tpb = kg.tokens_per_block
            if not tpb:
                return ()
            blocks = gpu_block_ids[kg.engine_group_idx]
            out.extend(blocks[r.cur_st // tpb : (r.cur_ed - 1) // tpb + 1])
    except (IndexError, TypeError, AttributeError):
        return ()
    return tuple(out)
```

This is strictly more precise than the whole-table hash: unrelated growth no longer
perturbs it, while a genuine reassignment of *that range's own* blocks still changes it
and re-scatters. It can only remove false negatives, never add a false positive — which
matters, because wrongly skipping a needed scatter would leave **unpopulated KV** rather
than merely costing work. Unavailable geometry yields the empty tuple, which never
matches a prior entry, so the fallback is "always re-scatter" — the old conservative
behaviour.

Net diff: one file, **+33/−12**.

## Side effect — and explicitly *not* the fix for it

The repeat call also re-reads object keys whose read locks the first call already
released after its scatter (`KEY_NOT_READABLE` → `scatter_ran=False` → the client
full-recomputes). Suppressing the redundant re-scatter should remove that read too.

**The underlying defect is a lock-lifecycle bug, not a dedup bug, and this PR does not
fix it.** The lookup reserves read locks for the *request*; the retrieve releases them
per *scatter*. So the storage manager — the single source of truth for object lifecycle —
stops recording a live reader while the request is still reading. CB compensates with
module-local state (`_cb_applied_match_ranges`, a **bounded LRU**) instead of the Session
lock model its own prefix leg already publishes via `record_prefetch_result`.

This PR makes that local state correct. It does **not** restore the invariant, and
specifically does not help:

* an **LRU eviction** of the applied-range entry, which silently reopens the gap;
* the **other two readers** of the same prefetched objects, which never consult CB's side
  table — `lmcache_driven_transfer.py:1450` (aux plane) and `server_transfer.py:247`.

The lifecycle fix belongs with the Session lock model (**#4852**): record the sparse
leg's locked keys on the Session, have the retrieve read-and-remove what it releases, and
release the remainder at session destroy with `read_locks=num_kv_readers`. Please don't
read this PR as closing that.

## Verification

The argument for this change is structural and needs no measurement: a hash over the
whole block table cannot answer *"did **this range's** destination move"*, because it also
changes when unrelated blocks are allocated. `1` skip hit against `3,328` failed reads is
the observable consequence.

An end-to-end run on minimax_m3 `bench_quality` (8xH200, TP=8, 20 samples) showed read
failures `1568 → 0` and degraded scatter calls `104/392 → 0/392`. **That comparison was
not single-variable** — the two images also differed in two unrelated lock changes — so it
is reported here as corroboration, not attribution. A controlled A/B differing only in
this commit is in progress and I will post it when it lands.

Full LMCache suite: **1849 passed, 41 skipped**. Lint clean.

No unit test: the computation is a few lines inside `cb_retrieve_pre_computed` and is not
reachable without standing up a GPU context, rope state and transfer module.

items.title: [Fix][CB] Reserve one sparse-leg read lock per KV reader, not one per key

labels.name: full
labels.description: Run comprehensive tests on this PR

items.body:
## What this PR does  
The sparse leg omitted `num_kv_readers`, so the spec defaulted to **1** read lock per key.
The prefix leg passes it.

This is harmless with sharded KV — one key per rank, each releasing its own. Under **MLA
the KV is stored once**, so every rank resolves to the same object key, dedup collapses
them to one, and that single lock goes to whichever rank retrieves first. The other
`tp-1` releases underflow and unpin the object while those ranks still need it.

items.title: [RFC][MP] Emit MP-server cache placements as engine-format KV events for KV-aware routers (llm-d)
items.body:
## Problem

KV-aware routers (llm-d, Dynamo) index KV placement from engine ZMQ events. In MP mode LMCache emits none: `take_events()` is a stub (`lmcache_mp_connector.py:1108`) and `enable_kv_events` has no reader outside `LMCacheEngine`, which MP never creates. The placement stream exists — it only flows to the coordinator.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  vllm[vLLM pod] -- ZMQ BlockStored/Removed --> epp[llm-d EPP index]
  vllm -. IPC .-> mp[lmcache server MP]
  mp -- POST /events --> coord[mp coordinator]
  mp x-. nothing .-x epp
```

Result: every LMCache tier is invisible to routing. #3532 is the llm-d user report; #4352 is the same gap for Dynamo.

## Goal / Non-goals

- Goal: llm-d routes to a pod whose node holds the prefix in LMCache, with hit-rate on par with vLLM's `OffloadingConnector` tier.
- LMCache emits hints only; it does not route (#4085 consensus). No data-path, protocol-semantics, or coordinator-contract changes.
- Scope: MP deployments **with a coordinator**. The coordinator is the single place that already holds the fleet's deduplicated, fenced placement stream; emitting from there is smaller and better-behaved than emitting from every MP server, so the server-side mount is not pursued.

## Key facts about the consumer (llm-d)

| llm-d needs | Consequence |
|---|---|
| topic `kv@<pod-id>@<model>` | segment 2 **is** the routing identity |
| `token_ids` in `BlockStored` | llm-d rehashes tokens; engine hash is opaque → LMCache chunk hash / `chunk_size=256` work as-is |
| `parent_hash` indexed or 0 | else event dropped |
| `medium` lowercase; unknown → weight 1.0 (=GPU) | needs an explicit weight |
| `BlockRemoved` with same `medium` | refcount dedup |
| `AllBlocksCleared` | pod-wide clear of the topic identity |
| no HMA fields | avoids strict gate |

Precedent: llm-d's own `llmd_fs_backend` publishes vLLM-format events from its own ZMQ socket, not through the engine.

## Design

### 1. Attribution: cache instance ≠ serving instance

An MP server is per node and serves N engines. A placement maps to the engines that can serve it:

| Placement | Topic identity | Credited to (llm-d/llm-d-router#2586) |
|---|---|---|
| L1, private L2 | the reporting server's `instance_id`, deployed as `node:<nodeName>` | engines on that node |
| shared L2 (fs / mooncake / S3) | `pool:<backend>` | all engines of the model |

The coordinator adds nothing to the identity: `--instance-id node:$NODE_NAME` on the MP server is the whole convention.

### 2. `ZmqKVEventPublisher` — a consumer behind the coordinator's ingest gate

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  s1[server node N] -- POST /events --> gate[EventGate]
  s2[server node M] -- POST /events --> gate
  gate --> dir[KeyDirectory]
  gate --> evict[FleetEvictionController]
  gate --> pub[ZmqKVEventPublisher]
  pub -- "kv@node:N@model / kv@pool:fs@model" --> epp[llm-d EPP]
  style pub stroke:#0f766e,stroke-width:2px
```

| vLLM field | Source |
|---|---|
| topic | `kv@<instance_id or pool:backend>@<model>` |
| `block_hashes` | `chunk_hash` (router truncates to 8 B) |
| `parent_hash` | previous chunk in the same `mp.tokens` binding (`CacheEventEntry.parent_hash_hex`, new) |
| `token_ids`, `block_size` | already on STORE entries; `chunk_size` |
| `medium` | `lmcache-l1`, `lmcache-l2-<backend>` — distinct from vLLM's `cpu` so weights are per LMCache tier |
| `BlockRemoved` | `DELETE` |
| `AllBlocksCleared` | `fence_instance` (incarnation bump, deregistration, heartbeat timeout), per model the instance published under |

Config: `lmcache coordinator --kv-events-endpoint tcp://*:5557 [--kv-events-replay-port N]`. MP servers are unchanged apart from carrying `parent_hash_hex` in the batches they already send.

What the gate gives the router for free: seq dedup (a retried batch is never re-published), incarnation fencing (a restart clears the node's entries before its new incarnation's first store), one subscription for the whole fleet.

## Failure semantics

Every hint is validate-on-use: the MP server's own lookup decides. Wrong hint = one sub-optimal route, never a correctness issue.

| Failure | Effect | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| lost `BlockStored` (bus drop / publish error) | false miss | next store re-emits |
| lost `BlockRemoved` | false hit → ordinary miss | LRU-bounded index; replay |
| store→evict window (#4085, @ardecode) | same as above | none; hints never pin memory |
| server restart | `AllBlocksCleared` | L2 re-announces |
| coordinator down | stream stalls, routing continues on stale index | `gap_detected` → replay on reconnect |
| shared L2 `delete` reported by one of several storing nodes | entry lingers under `pool:` until the others report | validate-on-use; follow-up: emit from directory transitions |

v1 hard requirements: identical `medium` for store/delete of one placement; no HMA fields; the publisher never blocks or fails the ingest path.

## Other routers (Dynamo, #4352)

Nothing in the wire format is router-specific, so Dynamo's indexer can parse the stream as-is. What differs is attribution: this design carries identity in the topic (`kv@<instance_id>@<model>` / `kv@pool:<backend>@<model>`) on one PUB endpoint, which llm-d keys on; Dynamo binds identity per registered endpoint, so one coordinator PUB would be credited to one worker. Bridging it is either Dynamo accepting topic identity / multi-worker registration (#4352 Proposal 1 blocker) or a publisher variant with one PUB socket per `instance_id` — the encoder and the coordinator-consumer mount are reusable, only the socket fan-out changes. If #4352 goes with the shared-cache pull path, the event stream is not needed there at all.

## Plan

| Step | Scope | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | publisher on the coordinator + config (PR #4768) | G1: golden fixtures decode in llm-d's `vllm_adapter` — **done**; coordinator e2e (`POST /events` → SUB, dedup, fence) — **done** |
| M2 | operator (`operator/`, separate PR): `LMCacheCoordinatorSpec.kvEvents {enabled, port, replayPort}` → flags + container/Service ports; engine DaemonSet gets `NODE_NAME` (downward API) and `--instance-id node:$(NODE_NAME)` | `extraArgs` alone cannot expose the ZMQ ports, and without the node identity topics are `kv@<uuid>@…` |
| M3 | single-node e2e with coordinator | G2: hit-rate ≥ 95% regardless of pod; no stale entries after evict/restart |
| M4 | multi-node | G3: shared L2 credited fleet-wide; replay restores index; coordinator kill is non-fatal |
| M5 | parity benchmark | G4: TTFT p99 ≤ 1.1× `OffloadingConnector` |

llm-d companion: llm-d/llm-d-router#2586 (pseudo-pods, `defaultWeight`, `lmcache-l1` weight).

## References

#4085, #4226, #4352, #3532

items.title: [CB] Add --enable-dedup-content to skip duplicate fingerprint registration

labels.name: full
labels.description: Run comprehensive tests on this PR

items.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

The blend V3 matcher dedups fingerprint registration by the caller's chunk content hash, which is prefix-chained: the same chunk text stored behind two different prefixes gets two different hashes and is indexed twice. The second registration takes over the probe-table slot, orphaning the first entry — it keeps a compact ID but can never match.

Adds `--enable-dedup-content` (opt-in, blend only): skip registering a chunk whose content fingerprint is already indexed, so the same text is indexed once and the first registration wins.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

Off by default; behavior is unchanged without the flag — the registration filter becomes an explicit loop yielding the same indices in the same order.

**If applicable**:
- [x] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [x] this PR contains unit tests

items.title: [CacheBlend] [blocker availability] Unbounded blend store fills the L2 disk and evicts the serving pods via node DiskPressure - no size cap
items.body:
# [CacheBlend] [blocker availability] Unbounded blend store fills the L2 disk and evicts the serving pods via node DiskPressure - no size cap

**Date:** 2026-08-20
**Verdict:** **CONFIRMED** (for the `fs_native`/GDS L2 backend, i.e. `GdsBackend`). **REFUTED by construction** for the alternative `LocalDiskBackend` path, which does enforce a hard cap + LRU eviction.
**Confidence:** High for the code mechanism (primary source, exact pinned versions, decisive "feature-absent" evidence) **and now for the unbounded write stream (MEASURED - §4: +10,923 store chunks over 100 novel queries, strictly linear, no plateau).** Medium only on the wall-clock time-to-outage (extrapolated, not driven to failure - deliberately, see Caveats).
**Severity:** High / availability blocker for any long-lived deployment using the `fs_native`/GDS L2 tier.

## Problem at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q["novel-ordering CacheBlend traffic"] --> W["about 109 new chunks written per query"]
  W --> G["GdsBackend fs_native: no size cap, no eviction"]
  G --> DSK["L2 disk grows without bound"]
  DSK --> F["disk fills"]
  F --> DP["node DiskPressure"]
  DP --> EV["kubelet evicts serving pods"]
  LDB["LocalDiskBackend: has cap plus LRU"] -.->|not the selected backend| G
```

## 1. Issue in one sentence

The `fs_native` L2 disk backend (LMCache `GdsBackend`) writes one file per distinct KV chunk **unconditionally, with no size cap and no eviction implemented at all**, so under CacheBlend novel-ordering traffic (which mints new distinct chunk keys continuously) the on-disk store grows without bound until the L2 filesystem/PVC fills, the node crosses the kubelet **DiskPressure** threshold, and the serving pods are evicted.

## 2. Versioning (exact)

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| LMCache source | `git describe` = **`v0.5.3-cu129-12-g9fc6e1af`**, commit **`9fc6e1afe83335a1c41b31662470fa115b2b6ac8`** |
| vLLM source | submodule `vLLM`, `git describe` = **`v0.26.1rc0-557-g436be94e13`**, commit **`436be94e135fd07fc94e4c165a1b6870af72bf31`** |
| Engine + blend-server image (ticket) | `lmcache/vllm-openai:v0.5.3` |
| CacheBlend plugin image (ticket) | `cacheblend-plugin:v0.5.3` |
| Model / quant / HW / TP (ticket bench env) | `gpt-oss-20b`, MXFP4, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, TP=1 |
| Cluster | a dev Kubernetes cluster |
| Relevant config defaults (LMCache `config.py`) | `chunk_size=256`; `max_local_disk_size` **default `0.0`**; `gds_buffer_size` default `None` (a *GPU staging* buffer, not a disk cap) |
| L2 backend under test | `l2.type: fs_native` (`use_gds: true`, `gds_backend: cufile`) → routes to LMCache `GdsBackend` |

## 3. Issue description (plain terms)

LMCache offers more than one on-disk ("L2") backend. They do **not** behave the same way with respect to disk safety:

- **`LocalDiskBackend`** - the "`local_disk`" path. It is created *only* when a positive `max_local_disk_size` is set, and it enforces that cap with LRU eviction on every write. **Bounded by construction.**
- **`GdsBackend`** - the "`gds_path`" path, selected by `l2.type: fs_native` (GDS/cuFile, or plain O_DIRECT/POSIX on a non-GDS filesystem). It has **no size/quota/cap parameter at all**, and eviction is **explicitly not implemented** - the code literally logs `"GDS Backend does not support eviction"`. Every distinct KV chunk is written as a new file and never reclaimed. **Unbounded.**

Any deployment that selects `l2.type: fs_native` uses the unbounded `GdsBackend`, and LMCache exposes no knob to bound it - the backend accepts no size parameter, so there is nothing a config layer could set.

Why it matters at production level: the L2 tier is a *shared node resource* (a dedicated NVMe device / PVC). When it fills, the failure is not a graceful cache miss - it is a **node-level `DiskPressure`** condition. The kubelet responds by evicting pods on that node. That takes down the serving engines (and can affect co-tenants on the same node), i.e. a self-inflicted availability outage that grows more likely the longer the deployment runs and the more distinct traffic it sees. CacheBlend traffic is the worst case for this: its whole point is *non-prefix* reuse over many document orderings, and each novel ordering produces new distinct chunk keys → the distinct-key set grows monotonically → the store grows monotonically.

## 4. How verified

### Method
Primary-source code read at the exact pinned commits above (no reliance on any existing doc). The claim is **structural** - the absence of a size cap and of eviction in a code path - so it is fully decidable from source. A live fill-to-failure run was deliberately **not** performed (it would harm the shared node; see Caveats for the safe signature recipe).

### CODE evidence - the `fs_native`/GDS backend has no cap and no eviction

**(a) Put is unconditional - no capacity/size check before writing.**
`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/gds_backend.py:591` `submit_put_task(...)` and `:615` `batched_submit_put_task(...)` go straight to `_async_save_bytes_to_disk` - there is no `max_cache_size`, no `current_cache_size`, no eviction loop anywhere in the write path:

```python
# gds_backend.py:591
def submit_put_task(self, key, memory_obj, on_complete_callback=None) -> Future:
    ...
    future = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
        self._async_save_bytes_to_disk(key, memory_obj, on_complete_callback),
        self.loop)
    return future
```
`_async_save_bytes_to_disk` (`:636`) `os.makedirs(...)` + `_save_gds(...)` writes a file per key. Every distinct key ⇒ one new file, always.

**(b) Eviction is explicitly not implemented.**
```python
# gds_backend.py:1105 / 1109  (pin/unpin)
# NOTE (ApostaC): Since gds doesn't have eviction now, we don't need
# to implement pin and unpin
```
```python
# gds_backend.py:1139-1140 and 1187-1188  (allocate / batched allocate)
if eviction:
    logger.warning("GDS Backend does not support eviction")
```

**(c) No disk-size cap knob exists for this backend.**
`GdsBackend.__init__` (`gds_backend.py:21`) reads only `gds_path`, `gds_path_sharding`, `use_gds`, `gds_backend`, `gds_buffer_size`. `gds_buffer_size` is a *GPU staging allocator* size (`gds_backend.py:1126`: `allocator_cls(config.gds_buffer_size * 1024**2)`), **not** a disk quota. There is no `max_*_disk_size` equivalent.

### CODE evidence - the *other* backend (`LocalDiskBackend`) IS bounded (why the claim is path-specific)

**(d) It only exists with a positive cap, and enforces it with LRU eviction.**
```python
# storage_backend/__init__.py:217
if (config.local_disk and config.max_local_disk_size > 0
        and "LocalDiskBackend" not in _skip):
    ... LocalDiskBackend(...)
```
```python
# local_disk_backend.py:174
self.max_cache_size = int(config.max_local_disk_size * 1024**3)
# local_disk_backend.py:346  (inside submit_put_task, under disk_lock)
while self.current_cache_size + required_size > self.max_cache_size:
    evict_keys = self.cache_policy.get_evict_candidates(self.dict, num_candidates=1)
    if not evict_keys:
        logger.warning("No eviction candidates found. Disk space under pressure.")
        evict_success = False
        break
    ...
```
So `LocalDiskBackend` cannot even be instantiated without a positive cap, and once running it evicts LRU entries to stay under that cap. This is the code that the ticket title implicitly assumes is missing - it exists, but on a **different backend than `fs_native`/GdsBackend**.

### CODE evidence - selecting fs_native routes to the unbounded backend

- `storage_backend/__init__.py:235` `if config.gds_path is not None: GdsBackend(...)` - an `fs_native` L2 config populates `gds_path`, so selecting it routes to the unbounded `GdsBackend`.

### RUN leg - safe store-growth SIGNATURE (MEASURED 2026-08-20; no disk-fill)
A fill-to-DiskPressure run is prohibited on the shared node, so instead the store's **write stream** was measured directly on a live blend server (gpt-oss-20b, one shared blend server, **100 novel-ordering queries**, scraping the server `/metrics` per batch) - the safe proxy for "does the store grow without bound":

| counter | start → end (100 novel queries) | Δ | per query |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total` | 26,179 → 37,102 | **+10,923** | ~109 chunks/query |
| `lmcache_mp_l1_evicted_chunks_total` | 24,228 → 35,254 | +11,026 | ~110/query |
| `lmcache_blend_lookup_stale_chunks_total` | 12,283 → 20,472 | +8,189 | ~82/query |
| `lmcache_mp_l1_memory_usage_bytes` | rose every batch (+3.4 GB, +1.6 GB, +2.1 GB … then tapering) | monotonic | - |

The store **writes ~109 new chunks per novel query and never stops** - `write_chunks_total` is strictly linear in query count (no dedup, no plateau-from-dedup). On the *bounded* L1 the write rate ≈ the evict rate (10,923 ≈ 11,026): L1 caps residency by evicting the warm set (this is also the decay mechanism of the sibling perf ticket). On the `fs_native`/GDS L2 `GdsBackend`, which has **no eviction** (code evidence above), that identical ~109-chunks/query write stream accumulates on disk **without bound** → the disk-fill/DiskPressure outcome is the L2 manifestation of exactly this measured write stream. This confirms the mechanism at runtime without ever approaching the disk limit.

## 5. Clues / evidence (summary)

| Signal | Backend | Location | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| No `max_cache_size` / eviction in write path | `GdsBackend` (fs_native) | `gds_backend.py:591`, `:615`, `:636` | writes every distinct key unconditionally |
| `"GDS Backend does not support eviction"` | `GdsBackend` | `gds_backend.py:1140`, `:1188` | nothing is ever reclaimed |
| `"gds doesn't have eviction now"` | `GdsBackend` | `gds_backend.py:1105`, `:1109` | pin/unpin are no-ops - no LRU machinery |
| No disk-cap config field | `GdsBackend` | `config.py:336-346`, `gds_backend.py:__init__` | `gds_buffer_size` is a GPU staging buffer, not a cap |
| Cap + LRU present, requires cap>0 to exist | `LocalDiskBackend` (not selected here) | `__init__.py:217`, `local_disk_backend.py:174,346` | the bounded path - not the one selected here |
| fs_native selects GdsBackend | LMCache | `storage_backend/__init__.py:235` | any deployment using `fs_native` gets the unbounded backend |

**Growth arithmetic (mechanism):** distinct chunks written = f(distinct chunk keys served). CacheBlend serves novel document orderings; with `chunk_size=256`, each novel ordering that isn't a pure prefix of a prior one produces fresh chunk keys. On-disk size ≈ (number of distinct chunks) × (serialized bytes per chunk). Because reclamation is 0, this is **strictly monotonic non-decreasing** for the life of the pod - it can only ever go up until the disk is full.

## 6. Chart

Measured cumulative store writes on the shared blend server over 100 novel-ordering queries - strictly linear (no dedup, no plateau):

```mermaid
xychart-beta
    title "Store write stream is unbounded (measured)"
    x-axis ["q0","q20","q40","q60","q80","q100"]
    y-axis "cumulative chunks written" 26000 --> 37500
    line [26179, 28364, 30549, 32734, 34918, 37102]
```

The bounded `LocalDiskBackend` (cap + LRU) would plateau; `GdsBackend` has no eviction, so this line only rises until the disk fills.

## 7. Root-cause analysis

The `GdsBackend` was built as a high-throughput GPU-Direct-Storage / O_DIRECT write path and, by the authors' own in-code notes, eviction was never added to it ("Since gds doesn't have eviction now…"). It therefore has neither a capacity parameter nor any reclamation policy: `submit_put_task` → `_async_save_bytes_to_disk` writes a file per key and returns. The sibling `LocalDiskBackend` carries the cap+LRU logic, but it is a *different* backend selected by a *different* config (`local_disk` + `max_local_disk_size>0`), not the `fs_native` path.

Selecting `l2.type: fs_native` routes to `GdsBackend`, which exposes no size limit (nor could a config layer add one - the backend accepts none). So a deployment using it has **no layer** that bounds the L2 store. Combined with CacheBlend's continuously-novel key stream, the store grows until the filesystem fills. On Kubernetes, a full node filesystem is a `DiskPressure` condition, which the kubelet resolves by evicting pods - hence the "evicts the serving pods" outcome in the title. The mechanism claimed by the ticket is real for the configuration that actually ships.

## 8. Caveats & unverified

- **Not driven to failure (by design).** The DiskPressure/eviction *outcome* is inferred from the standard kubelet behavior for a full node filesystem, not reproduced - reproducing it would degrade the shared dev node. The store-*growth* half is code-certain; the eviction half is the well-known kubelet consequence of it.
- **Time-to-outage not quantified.** Wall-clock time to fill depends on serialized bytes/chunk (model dims, `chunk_size=256`, dtype), L2 device capacity, and traffic novelty rate - none measured here. The chart axes are therefore unitless.
- **Whether an *external* backend (RESP/remote) has its own server-side cap** is out of scope; this report covers the on-node `fs_native`/GDS L2 (`GdsBackend`). A `resp` (Redis-protocol) remote backend's capacity would be governed by that server, not this code.
- **`use_gds: false` (plain O_DIRECT fs_native) uses the same `GdsBackend` class** and the same no-cap/no-evict paths - it does not change the verdict.

**Single cleanest next check (safe, GPU-light, does NOT approach disk-full):** deploy one throwaway CacheBlend engine with a *small* L1 and an `fs_native` L2 pointed at a **small, isolated, bounded** scratch dir; drive N successive *novel-ordering* batches (well short of filling the dir); after each batch record `ls "$BASE_PATH" | wc -l` and `du -sh "$BASE_PATH"`. Expect a **strictly increasing** file count and byte total with zero decreases across batches (no eviction). Fit the slope to bytes-per-distinct-chunk, then divide real L2 capacity by that slope to project time/volume-to-DiskPressure - extrapolate to the outage; never cause it. Tear down the engine and delete the scratch dir afterward.

### Reproduction pointers (so this file stands alone)
- Code: `LMCache` @ `9fc6e1af`; read `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/gds_backend.py` (lines 591, 615, 636, 1105, 1139, 1187), `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_disk_backend.py` (lines 174, 346), `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/__init__.py` (lines 217, 235), `lmcache/v1/config.py` (lines 90, 113, 336-346, 1203-1205).

*Every fact above is labeled: CODE-VERIFIED = read from source at the pinned commit; INFERRED = the kubelet DiskPressure→eviction consequence and the time-to-outage; nothing here is MEASURED from a live run (none was performed).*

items.title: [CacheBlend] [blocker perf] Non-prefix reuse decays to ~1× under sustained novel RAG - the blend store is prefix-chained and unbounded while the lookup is content-addressed
items.body:
# [CacheBlend] [blocker perf] Non-prefix reuse decays to ~1× under sustained novel RAG - the blend store is prefix-chained and unbounded while the lookup is content-addressed

**Date:** 2026-08-20
**Verdict:** **CONFIRMED** - reproduced live and grounded in source.
**Confidence:** High (MEASURED decay curve on dev + CODE-VERIFIED mechanism at the pinned commit).
**Severity:** blocker (perf) - CacheBlend fails to sustain its value under exactly the workload it exists for (non-prefix RAG recombination); the win is a freshly-warmed burst, not steady state.

## Problem at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Q["Novel RAG query: 14 docs, shuffled order"]
  Q --> LK["LOOKUP: content-addressed hash, offset-tolerant"]
  Q --> ST["STORE: prefix-chained hash, unconditional"]
  LK --> HIT["finds each doc KV at any position"]
  ST --> NEW["about 112 brand-new keys per novel query"]
  HIT --> BURST["warm burst 2-4x"]
  NEW --> FLOOD["unbounded store floods L1"]
  FLOOD --> EVICT["LRU evicts the warm doc chunks"]
  EVICT --> DECAY["reuse decays to ~1x within ~60-90 queries"]
  BURST -.->|eroded by| DECAY
```

## 1. Versioning

| Component | Value |
|---|---|
| LMCache | commit `9fc6e1af` (`v0.5.3-cu129-12-g9fc6e1af`) |
| vLLM (bundles the MP KV connector) | commit `436be94e` (`v0.26.1rc0-557-g436be94e13`) |
| Serving/engine + blend-server image | `lmcache/vllm-openai:v0.5.3` |
| CacheBlend plugin (webhook-injected) | `cacheblend-plugin:v0.5.3` |
| Model | `openai/gpt-oss-20b` (MoE, MXFP4, hybrid sliding+full attention → forces the MP connector) |
| Hardware | 1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB), TP=1 |
| Cluster | a dev Kubernetes cluster |
| Blend config | `chunk_size=256`, `recomp_ratio=0.15`, `check_layer=1`, eviction LRU, `max_workers=4` |
| Blend L1 (DRAM) | two runs: **100 GB** and **20 GB** |
| Connector | CBKVConnector over the MP connector (`kv_role=kv_both`), CUSTOM attention backend, hostIPC (webhook-injected) |

The model is gpt-oss-20b (not 120b); it shares gpt-oss's hybrid-SWA architecture, so it exercises the **same MP-connector store path** the defect lives in. The absolute burst magnitude is smaller than a 120B would show, but the decay behavior is architecture-general.

## 2. Issue description (plain terms)

CacheBlend's job is to reuse each retrieved document's KV **regardless of the document's position** in a RAG prompt, so that re-ordered / re-combined documents skip most of prefill. Its **lookup** does exactly that - it is content-addressed and position-independent. But its **store** reuses the ordinary prefix-cache write: it persists position-dependent KV keyed by a **rolling, prefix-chained hash**, unconditionally, on every request. Under sustained *novel-ordering* RAG traffic (the normal production pattern for RAG: each query retrieves a different combination/order of documents), every request mints a fresh batch of brand-new, un-dedupable keys. Those keys can only ever serve a future **contiguous-prefix** hit - which never happens on novel RAG - and they are useless to the content-addressed blend matcher, yet they pile into the shared L1 without bound. Once L1 saturates, LRU evicts the **warm document chunks** (the only thing the matcher can actually reuse), so the speedup **decays from a post-warm burst down to the cold baseline within a few dozen queries.** Nothing is functionally wrong; the store/lookup **asymmetry** is the defect. Production impact: any benchmark that re-warms before each measurement reports the burst (e.g. 4–6×) and completely misses that steady-state throughput under real sustained novel traffic falls back to ~1×.

## 3. How verified

### Runtime (MEASURED, dev)
- Deployed a `CacheBlendEngine` blend server + a webhook-injected gpt-oss-20b vLLM engine (config above).
- Built a corpus of **112 docs × 2048 tokens** (2048 = 8 × 256, so docs are chunk-aligned - this isolates the decay from any chunk-seam effect). Each query = **14 docs concatenated in a fresh shuffled order that never repeats** (never-reset RNG). `max_tokens=1` (prefill/TTFT only), concurrency 1.
- Metric = **prefill throughput vs a true-COLD baseline** (fresh, never-cached documents) - the only trustworthy signal (the built-in hit-counters mislabel blend reuse). Cold baseline measured n=3.
- Ran the full corpus warm pass once, then sustained novel-ordering batches (32 queries/batch), scraping the blend server's store/eviction counters per batch.

### Code (CODE-VERIFIED, commit `9fc6e1af` / `436be94e`)
- Lookup is content-addressed and offset-tolerant; store is prefix-chained; the MP connector stores unconditionally. Decisive lines quoted in §5.

## 4. Clues / evidence - measured decay

**COLD baseline (n=3):** 17,033 tok/s (14,912 / 18,096 / 18,092) - tight.

**Run A - blend L1 = 100 GB (full burst→decay):**

| novel batch | throughput (tok/s) | vs COLD | p50 (ms) | eviction Δ (chunks) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 (warm burst) | 76,265 | **4.48×** | 300 | 8,443 |
| 1 | 39,678 | **2.33×** | 715 | 9,409 |
| 2 | 22,436 | **1.32×** | 1,123 | 10,924 |
| 3 | 18,249 | **1.07×** | 1,585 | 11,639 |
| 4 | 18,450 | 1.08× | 1,585 | 11,829 |
| 5 | 18,069 | 1.06× | 1,586 | 21,013 |
| 6 | 18,245 | 1.07× | 1,585 | 23,200 |
| 7 | 23,815 | 1.40× | 1,585 | 32,586 |
| 8 | 77,273 | 4.54× | 317 | 24,583 |
| 9 | 30,780 | 1.81× | 957 | 14,663 |

Clean monotonic collapse **4.48× → 2.33× → 1.32× → 1.07×** over 3 batches, then a noisy cold-floor. Eviction Δ climbs monotonically (8.4k → 32.6k) while per-batch store Δ stays roughly constant (~1,500–1,700) - i.e. the store keeps adding fresh un-dedup'd chunks every batch and the cache churns them against the warm set. (Batches 7–9 spike back up: stochastic recurrence - some random 14-doc draws happen to land on docs still resident from a recent batch. This is not monotonic-to-zero; it's a noisy cold-floor with occasional transient re-hits, consistent with the mechanism.)

**Run B - blend L1 = 20 GB (smaller cache saturates in one batch):**

| novel batch | vs COLD | eviction Δ |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1.49× | 8,919 |
| 1 | 1.08× | 9,721 |
| 2 | 1.07× | 13,608 |
| 3 | 1.07× | 18,562 |
| 4 | 1.12× | 17,944 |
| 5 | 1.06× | 19,682 |

A smaller L1 both **lowers the burst** (less warm headroom) and **decays in a single batch** (saturates immediately) - exactly what an unbounded store flooding a fixed cache predicts. The L1-size dependence is itself confirmation of the root cause.

### Chart
Prefill throughput vs COLD per novel-ordering batch (L1=100GB; COLD baseline 17,033 tok/s):

```mermaid
xychart-beta
    title "Non-prefix reuse decays: speedup vs cold per novel batch"
    x-axis ["b0","b1","b2","b3","b4","b5","b6","b7","b8","b9"]
    y-axis "x vs cold" 0 --> 5
    line [4.48, 2.33, 1.32, 1.07, 1.08, 1.06, 1.07, 1.40, 4.54, 1.81]
```

## 5. Decisive code lines (commit `9fc6e1af`)

**Lookup is content-addressed + offset-tolerant.** `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/blend_v3.py`, `match_sub_sequence`:
```python
rolling = rolling_hash_windows_numba(arr, self.chunk_size, self._BASE)   # stride-1 window at EVERY position
...  # direct-address probe over all positions → a chunk matches wherever its content appears
```
The index is populated by `on_new_token_hashes` via `chunk_hash_windows_numba(arr, self.chunk_size, ...)` - **non-overlapping** 256-token chunks keyed by content.

**Store is prefix-chained (position-dependent).** `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/session.py` (~L116-122):
```python
prefix = self.last_prefix_hash if self.last_prefix_hash is not None else self.hasher.none_hash
h = self.hasher.hash_tokens(chunk, prefix)   # chunk key hashes the chunk PLUS all preceding tokens
self.last_prefix_hash = h
```

**The MP connector stores every request unconditionally.** `lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_metadata.py` - `GetStoreMetadata` (def ~L176) takes only `(tracker, tokens_per_chunk, tokens_per_block)` and gates solely on new-chunk count (no dedup, no skip gate); both call sites in the connector (`_process_new_requests`, `_process_cached_requests`) invoke it and add the STORE op whenever chunks exist. A novel 14-doc ordering therefore mints ~112 brand-new prefix-chained keys/query (×object-groups ×ranks), none of which dedup.

**Consequence:** the store set is unbounded (unique per preceding-context → effectively `C(112,14)·14!` distinct keys), it floods L1, and LRU evicts the warm document chunks the matcher needs.

## 6. Root-cause analysis

One defect: **the store key-space and the lookup key-space are asymmetric.**
- Lookup keys are **content-only** → bounded by corpus size, reusable at any position. Correct.
- Store keys are **prefix-chained** → unbounded (one new set per novel ordering), and useful only for a contiguous-prefix hit that never occurs in RAG.

Every novel query writes junk that (a) never serves a future novel query and (b) evicts the genuinely reusable warm chunks. So the reuse the matcher *could* deliver is continuously destroyed by the store path feeding the same L1. The burst exists only while the warm set is still resident; sustained novel traffic without continuous re-warm drives it to the cold floor. Larger L1 delays the collapse; it does not prevent it (the store set is unbounded).

## 7. Regime (never a flat multiplier)

- **Post-warm burst:** ~2–4.5× (here 4.48× at L1=100 GB, 1.49× at L1=20 GB) - transient.
- **Sustained uniform-novel:** decays to **~1.0–1.1×** (cold floor) within ~1–3 batches (~30–90 queries).
- **Sustained with recurrence:** partial - batches that happen to re-draw resident docs spike (up to 4.5× here), so skewed/popularity-heavy RAG sustains *some* reuse; uniform-novel is the worst case.

Report the regime; do not quote the burst as the headline number.

## 8. Caveats & the single cleanest next check

- **Model:** measured on gpt-oss-20b, not 120b - the decay mechanism is architecture-general (same MP store path), but absolute burst magnitudes differ. INFERRED that 120b shows a larger burst with the same decay shape.
- **Docs were chunk-aligned (2048 tok):** this deliberately removes any 256-chunk seam effect so the decay reflects only the store flood. Real unpadded RAG would show *additional* reuse loss on top.
- **Cleanest next check:** apply a save-skip gate to the MP connector (mirroring the single-process `lmcache.skip_save` path), warm once, then serve read-only, and re-run this exact driver. Expected pass = store Δ → 0 after warm, eviction Δ flat, and the burst **holding** across all batches instead of decaying. That both proves the root cause and validates the fix.

labels.name: full
labels.description: Run comprehensive tests on this PR

items.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

The coordinator knows how many bytes each MP server holds, but not how many it *can* hold. This adds the missing denominator and serves the join over HTTP.

Each MP server declares per-compartment capacity (L1 pool per backing medium, one entry per L2 adapter) on the cache-event stream it already publishes — once at startup, then on every topology change. The coordinator joins those against the per-instance totals `CacheUsageManager` already tracks from the same stream. A compartment is keyed `(tier, backend)`, the same axis cache events tag placements with.

**HTTP API**

`GET /instances/usage` — whole fleet. `GET /instances/{instance_id}/usage` — one server, same shape; `404` if the coordinator knows nothing about the id.

```
{
  "instances": [
    {"instance_id": "mp-1", "registered": true, "declared_capacity": true,
     "modules": [
       {"tier": "l1", "backend": "dram", "shared": false,
        "used_bytes": 32212254720, "capacity_bytes": 42949672960, "usage_ratio": 0.75},
       {"tier": "l2", "backend": "fs", "shared": false,
        "used_bytes": 12884901888, "capacity_bytes": 0, "usage_ratio": null}
     ]}
  ],
  "shared_modules": [
    {"tier": "l2", "backend": "s3", "shared": true,
     "used_bytes": 9663676416, "capacity_bytes": 0, "usage_ratio": null}
  ]
}
```

Conventions:

- `usage_ratio` is `null`, never a number, when no capacity was declared — the common case (`fs`, `mooncake`, `p2p`, `sagemaker` expose no capacity setting). `null` means *unknown*, not *empty*.
- Ratios above `1.0` are not clamped; over-cap means the declaration is wrong, and hiding it hides a misconfiguration.
- Shared pools (one S3 bucket, N mounts) are counted once under `shared_modules`. Capacity is reported only when every declaring server agrees; disagreement reads as undeclared.

Read-only. No eviction, no throttling, no derived LOW/HIGH/CRITICAL — with most L2 backends declaring nothing, a normalized level would be confidently wrong on most deployments.

**Why capacity rides the event stream**

Capacity is configuration: it changes at boot and reconfiguration, not per operation, and carries no `ObjectKey` for the ingest gate to dedup on. Reports are whole declarations, never deltas — which is what makes a lossy channel acceptable, since a dropped report is repaired by the next one. Unsent reports are held across publish failures. Fencing is on `(incarnation, revision)`; revision alone restarts with the process, so a restarted server's first report would look stale forever.

Registration deliberately carries no capacity. Registration and event reporting are separately configurable, so a server registering without event reporting would declare capacity whose usage never arrives — every compartment reading a confident `0.0`, indistinguishable from empty.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- Addresses all three review comments: endpoints under `/instances/usage`, `L1Manager.get_configured_capacity_bytes()` removed, capacity event-driven only.
- One correction: nothing was polling periodically. `memory_capacities` was a probe called once per registration. The real problem was two paths for one fact.
- `CacheEventSink.publish()` gains `capacity_reports` — breaking signature change for out-of-tree implementers.
- `configured_l1_capacity_bytes()` in `distributed/config.py` is now the single derivation of L1 size, replacing a duplicate in `usage_telemetry/messages.py`. L1 only — L2 isn't uniformly derivable from config (four field names, two units, 21 adapters; `raw_block`/`nixl_store` discover theirs at runtime), so L2 goes through each adapter's `get_usage().total_capacity_bytes`.
- Open question: `shared_modules` is fleet-scoped but served from `/instances`. A separate route is cleaner REST; one round trip is what a fleet view wants. Happy either way.
- Early commit subjects describe capacity at registration; later commits replace that. Final state is event-only.

**If applicable**:

- [x] user facing changes — docs added (`docs/source/mp/coordinator.rst`, `docs/design/v1/mp_coordinator/memory_pressure.md`)
- [x] unit tests

Cut the `jq` ranking example and the standalone `curl` invocations — reviewers can infer both from the schema. If you want it shorter still, the "Why capacity rides the event stream" section could collapse to two sentences, but it's the part most likely to preempt a review round.

items.title: [Coordinator][Refactor]: cache-event ingest layer and fleet controllers

labels.name: full
labels.description: Run comprehensive tests on this PR

items.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Three seams in the mp coordinator were folded together; this splits them.

- The key directory was both the placement store *and* the fencing/dedup gate every cache event had to pass through. It becomes an ordinary `CacheEventConsumer`; admission moves to a new `ingest/` layer (`EventGate` + `CacheEventBroadcaster`).
- `cache_control/` + the eviction manager become `controllers/`. `FleetEvictionController` owns the quota registry, the usage view, and its own control loop — previously a `while True` in `create_app`'s lifespan.
- `POST /directory/events` → `POST /events`, in its own `events_api.py`: the stream feeds every consumer of it, not just the directory.

Also drops the startup L2 resync, so `POST /events` is the coordinator's single ingest path.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

Two behavior changes, both deliberate:

1. **Endpoint rename is a breaking wire change.** Both sides move together in-tree (`HttpCacheEventSink` posts the new path), but a fleet upgraded piecemeal will silently stop reporting — old MP servers get a 404 and the sink drops the batch.

2. **Startup resync is removed**, along with `LMCACHE_MP_COORDINATOR_ENABLE_STARTUP_RESYNC`, `RESYNC_POLL_INTERVAL`, `RESYNC_MAX_WAIT`, and `RESYNC_PAGE_SIZE`. A restarted coordinator now rebuilds usage purely from the event stream, so per-salt totals start at zero and climb rather than being seeded from a live server's `GET /cache/objects`. Unquota'd salts stay exempt until the quota controller arms a default limit, so a cold coordinator still cannot mass-evict — but it will under-evict until the stream catches up. This removes the gate's second, cursor-free `reconcile()` door; event replay from a durable transport remains the intended answer for gap recovery.

`GET /directory/stats` keeps its exact response shape; the per-instance row is now joined at the API layer from the gate's stream cursor and the directory's L1 key count.

**If applicable**:

items.title: [RFC][MP Coordinator] Refactor the mp coordinator into ingest, key directory, controllers and persistence
items.body:
## Summary

The coordinator has grown one capability at a time. Each capability added its own wiring, so today the key directory, the usage view, the eviction LRU, the pin table, the dispatcher and the resync pass are tangled in ways that make the next capability harder than the last.

This RFC proposes four layers:

- **Ingest** — HTTP or a message queue delivers events; one **event gate** fences, dedups, handles gaps and owns the stream position; one **broadcaster** fans applied batches out.
- **Key directory** — the placement index and the token bindings. It is the one per-key store, and it has to exist anyway because the read APIs are served from it.
- **Controllers** — each builds exactly the state it needs from the event stream, plans against the directory, and dispatches actions to MP servers. The eviction controller is the first one; others follow the same shape.
- **Persistence** — a **checkpointer** that periodically snapshots the directory plus opted-in controller state, and a **metadata persister** that writes operator intent when it changes.

Startup resync goes away. Recovery is checkpoint plus replay from the durable transport.

This is not one PR. The goal is to agree on the shape, then land it in small steps, each useful on its own.

## Motivation

How the pieces connect today:

```text
  POST /directory/events ─┐
  startup resync ─────────┼─►  KeyDirectory  ─►  broadcaster ─►  L2UsageManager
  checkpoint restore ─────┘    fencing                            L2EvictionManager
                               dedup / gap                          LRU order
                               placements                           pin table
                               token bindings                       eviction dispatch
                                                                    (reads the usage view
                                                                     mid-batch)

  outbound:  eviction → DELETE /cache/objects
             prefetch → POST /cache/prefetches      three separate HTTP callers
             resync   → GET  /cache/objects
```

Three ways in, three ways out, and one class holding five unrelated jobs.

Concrete problems in the code today, not hypotheticals:

**1. Consumers read each other.** `L2EvictionManager.consume` asks `L2UsageManager` whether a key still has bytes, in the middle of the same batch. It works only because `create_app` registers the usage view first, which is documented in a comment. Any new consumer has to know this rule, and the rule is invisible at the call site.

**2. The same state is stored twice.** `L2UsageManager` keeps `_placement_sizes` and `_key_sizes` — sizes the key directory already holds on every placement. It also re-implements the directory's placement identity (`owner = "" if batch.shared else instance_id`), because it receives the raw batch rather than what the directory decided. Two copies of one rule, and two copies of a map the size of the fleet's key space.

**3. Fencing is invisible.** Incarnation fencing drops an instance's old L1 placements inside the directory. No consumer hears about it. That is harmless today because every consumer filters to L2, and it blocks the first consumer that cares about L1.

**4. Recency does not survive a restart.** The checkpoint replays stores grouped by placement identity, so after a restart the LRU order is replay order, not real recency. The directory already stores `last_access`, so the information is there — it is just not used.

**5. The eviction manager does five jobs.** It tracks the LRU, decides when to fire, picks victims, picks a target server, and dispatches HTTP. It also owns the pin table, which the delete API reaches into. Adding L1 eviction, private-L2 eviction, or demote/promote to this class means multiplying conditionals inside it.

**6. There are three ways in and three ways out.** Events arrive by HTTP, by checkpoint restore, and by resync — each wired separately in `app.py`. Eviction, prefetch and resync each build their own outbound HTTP calls.

**7. Resync is the wrong recovery mechanism.** It pages through a live MP server's `GET /cache/objects` listing. `key_directory.md` already says the intended answer is replaying the event stream from the transport's retention. Once events live in a durable pipe, resync is redundant.

## Proposed direction

The way in — MP servers to state:

```text
  MP server
    storage layer  ->  event bus  ->  cache event subscriber
                                              |
                                              |  cache events
                                              v
  MP coordinator, ingest layer
    HTTP ingest                            MQ ingest
    POST /cache-events                     Kafka: seek + lag
              \                                /
               +--------------+---------------+
                              v
                         Event Gate
              fence / seq dedup / gap -> seek / cursor
                              |
                    AppliedBatch = batch + effects
                              v
                      Event Broadcaster
                              |
              +---------------+----------------+
              v                                v
        Key Directory                     Controllers
   placement index                    eviction controller
     objectkey -> placements            usage view, quota, order
   token bindings                     other controllers
     chunk_hash -> token_ids,           L1, demote, promote, ...
     offsets
   serves /directory/* read APIs
```

The way out — controllers to MP servers, and what survives a restart:

```text
   controller
     fold   its own aggregates, from the applied event stream
     plan   read the key directory for per-key facts        <-- the only cross-read
     act    dispatch to the MP server that holds the key
                              |
                              v
        MP server     DELETE /cache/objects
                      POST /cache/prefetches
                              |
                              +--> results return as ordinary events through ingest

   persistence layer
     checkpointer        periodic: key directory + opted-in controller state,
                         plus the stream position that state matches
     metadata persister  on change: quotas + pins
                         restored before replay, so restored keys are pinned
```

### Ingest: one gate, two ways in

Split what the key directory does today into two things:

- **Event gate** — per-instance fencing, sequence dedup, gap handling, and the stream position. There can only be one of these per stream, and it is the only thing that decides what "applied" means.
- **Key directory** — the state itself, registered as a consumer like any other.

Both ingest paths converge before the gate, so nothing downstream knows how an event arrived. The difference is capability, not code path: MQ ingest can `seek`, so a detected gap becomes a rewind; HTTP ingest cannot, so a gap stays a gap and the checkpoint is that deployment's only recovery.

```text
EventSource:
  start(sink)
  seek(positions)
  lag()
  stop()
```

The ingest endpoint is renamed `POST /directory/events` → `POST /cache-events`. The old name implied the directory owns ingestion; it does not — the gate does, and the directory is one of several consumers.

The gate should also emit control events, so consumers can react to things they cannot see today:

```text
FENCE(instance_id, incarnation)     an instance restarted; drop its L1 placements
DROP_INSTANCE(instance_id)          instance deregistered or timed out
```

Topic layout: **one topic**, carrying every event type, time-retained, keyed by `instance_id`. That keeps the semantics the coordinator already has — a single per-instance order across all event types, one consumer group, one cursor, one retention knob, and no change to what the MP-server subscriber emits. Splitting placements onto a compacted topic would allow bootstrap-from-topic and would let catch-up skip accesses, but it costs the total order between a store and an access of the same key, and doubles the operational surface. It stays available later if catch-up time becomes the bottleneck.

Two consequences follow from one topic, and both should be written down:

- **The checkpoint is required, not an optimization.** Nothing else can rebuild state older than retention.
- **Catch-up cost is total event volume since the checkpoint.** So the snapshot interval is what bounds recovery time, and retention must comfortably exceed the longest expected coordinator downtime.

### Key directory: the one per-key store

The directory holds the placement index (`objectkey -> placements`, with size and recency) and the token bindings (`chunk_hash -> token_ids, offsets`, which also back blend lookup).

It is not privileged because it is the directory. It is privileged because `/directory/lookup`, `/directory/keys`, `/directory/stats` and `/directory/blend-lookup` mean a per-key store has to exist regardless of what any control logic wants. Since one exists, no second one should.

### Controllers own their state

There is no shared views layer. A controller subscribes to the applied stream and builds exactly what it needs.

```text
CacheController:
  name
  consume(applied)                 fold: update this controller's own aggregates
  plan(context) -> [action]        pure: read the directory, decide
```

Today's `L2UsageManager` + `L2EvictionManager` collapse into one **eviction controller** that owns the per-salt usage view, the quota table, and its ordering structure — and nothing else. A future L1 controller owns its own aggregates. Neither reads the other.

Two rules keep this from turning into duplicated state:

**Fold from the event. Plan from the directory.** During `consume`, a controller touches only what is in the batch — no reads of the directory, no reads of another controller. That is what makes folds order-independent, and it is why the applied batch carries effects (`bytes_delta`, `key_now_empty`) computed once by the gate rather than re-derived per controller. During `plan`, the controller reads the directory freely; steady state, no ordering question, and every answer is a hint validated at the owning MP server anyway.

**Anything O(keys) lives in the directory.** A controller may hold aggregates — per-salt totals, per-instance counters, cooldowns, in-flight sets — and an ordering structure when it needs one. It must not hold a second map of the key space. If a controller needs a per-key fact the directory does not carry (hit counts for an LFU-style policy, say), the field is added to the directory, not to the controller. At fleet scale a per-key map is gigabytes: one is a cost of doing business, three is a bug.

The cases where a controller reads the directory are concrete: sizing a plan, resolving which instance holds a key before dispatch (mandatory once private L2 and L1 are in play, where "any holder" is no longer true), deciding whether a demote is a copy or a drop, ranking candidates when the controller keeps no ordering structure, and skipping victims whose last placement is already gone.

Ordering discipline is therefore a property of a controller, not of a shared index. LRU reads `last_access`, LFU reads hit counts, a size-aware policy weighs bytes. `lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/` already defines `EvictionPolicy` (`on_keys_created` / `on_keys_touched` / `on_keys_removed` / `get_eviction_actions`) with LRU and isolated-LRU implementations, and the current eviction manager already delegates to it — a controller's ordering structure is that interface fed by the event stream instead of by local storage callbacks.

### Controllers act, and the loop closes through ingest

A controller resolves the target instance from the registry and calls that MP server's existing endpoint — `DELETE /cache/objects` for eviction, `POST /cache/prefetches` for a warm-up. There is no generic command channel and no per-instance connection state.

Controllers never mutate coordinator state directly as a result of dispatching. The key leaves the eviction order when its delete event comes back through ingest. That is what makes at-least-once dispatch safe, and it is the property to preserve for every future action type: **dispatch is a request, the stream is the truth.**

Actions want a shared vocabulary once there is more than one kind:

```text
action     DELETE | DEMOTE | PROMOTE
keys
source     (tier, backend, scope = fleet | instance_id)
target     for DEMOTE / PROMOTE
reason     quota | capacity | hotness
```

Chunking to `MAX_DELETE_BATCH`, in-flight suppression and retry policy are the same for every controller, so they belong in one shared dispatch helper rather than being re-implemented per controller. Whether that helper also merges conflicting actions across controllers — the same key targeted for DELETE by one and PROMOTE by another — is an open question below; it cannot be answered with only one controller.

### Persistence: two components, split by write trigger

- **Checkpointer** — periodic. Snapshots the key directory plus any controller state that opted in, together with the stream position that state matches. Large, binary, derived, best-effort: an unusable checkpoint starts the coordinator cold and a failed write retries next tick.
- **Metadata persister** — on change. Quotas and pins: small, JSON, operator intent that nothing can rebuild. Written by the API calls that change it, restored before replay so restored keys enter the eviction order already pinned.

The hard rule for the checkpointer: **the recorded position must never be ahead of the state.** Behind is fine — replaying a few batches twice is deduped by the sequence cursor. Ahead is a permanent hole. All sections restore at the same position, or controllers disagree with the directory about what they have seen.

Most controller state needs no section, because it is rebuildable by scanning the restored directory at boot: per-salt totals are one pass, LRU order is a sort by `last_access`. A controller opts into a section only when its state is neither derivable from the directory nor operator intent — an accumulated hit count, a decayed score with its `as_of` stamp. State that is merely convenient — cooldowns, in-flight sets — is dropped on purpose.

### Readiness is a condition, not a component

Resync doubles as warm-up today. Remove it and a fresh coordinator serves a half-built view while the metadata persister has already restored quotas — including a default limit of 0, which means "evict everything unquota'd". A controller planning in that window would order a fleet-wide eviction.

The fix is one check, not a module: the scheduler does not call `plan()` while `gate.lag()` is over threshold, and the same value backs the readiness probe.

### Ownership

```text
Ingest:
  owns the stream position, fencing, dedup, gap repair, fan-out

Key directory:
  the one per-key store; placement index + token bindings; serves the read APIs

Controllers:
  own their aggregates; fold from events; plan from the directory; dispatch actions

Persistence:
  checkpointer       = directory + opted-in controller state + position
  metadata persister = operator intent, on change
```

## Relation to existing work

- #4065 — native coordinator mode as the distributed control plane. This RFC is about the module shape inside the coordinator, and should make a native port easier: ingest, directory, controllers and persistence are separable units with narrow contracts.
- #4226 — control-plane RFC / key directory milestones.
- #4275, #4292 — fleet-wide key directory and MP-server event emission.
- #4310 — quota accounting routed through the cache-event stream.
- #4404 — token directory built from cache events.
- #4438 — fleet blend lookup served from the key directory.
- #4027 — eviction dispatch chunking and the default quota limit.
- #3978, #3990 — coordinator pin/unpin and token-based delete, the callers of the pin table.
- The checkpoint/restore work on `feat/directory-snapshot`.

## Proposed work plan

Each milestone is shippable on its own. The first four are worth doing even if the rest never happens.

### Milestone 1: quotas and pins become durable controller state

Pins and quotas are declared through the `DurableComponent` protocol and written by the metadata persister on change. The delete API asks the owning controller instead of reaching into an eviction internal.

### Milestone 2: applied batches carry effects

The gate computes `bytes_delta` and `key_now_empty` once and passes them to consumers. No consumer reads another consumer. Registration order stops being load-bearing.

### Milestone 3: recency survives restart

Replay the checkpoint in `last_access` order. Small change in `persistence/checkpoint.py`, fixes a live gap.

### Milestone 4: collapse the L2 managers into the eviction controller

`L2UsageManager` and `L2EvictionManager` become one eviction controller holding the usage view, the quota table and an ordering structure. Per-key sizes come from the directory. This is where the duplicated key-space map disappears.

### Milestone 5: split the event gate from the key directory

Fencing, dedup and gap state move to the gate. The directory registers as a consumer. `FENCE` and `DROP_INSTANCE` control events are added. Checkpoint restore and resync feed the gate instead of writing state directly.

### Milestone 6: ingest sources and stream position

Add the `EventSource` seam and rename the endpoint to `POST /cache-events`. Store the stream position in the checkpointer. HTTP ingest becomes the first source, with `lag() == 0` and a no-op `seek()`.

### Milestone 7: MQ ingest, lag gate, delete resync

Kafka source on one topic keyed by instance. A gap becomes a seek. The scheduler holds `plan()` while lag is over threshold. Only after this lands does resync get deleted.

### Milestone 8: shared action vocabulary and dispatch

Move chunking, in-flight suppression and retry into one dispatch helper, and introduce the action vocabulary. Land this with the second controller, so it is designed against more than one example.

## Open questions

- Who owns pins once a second controller needs them? They sit naturally in the eviction controller today, but an L1 controller and the delete API both want them, which argues for a small shared registry instead.
- Should the shared dispatch helper also merge conflicting actions across controllers — same key, DELETE from one and PROMOTE from another — or should controllers be required to not overlap by construction?
- Should `DELETE` events carry `size_bytes`? The emitter knows it, and byte accounting would drop to O(salts) with no per-key sizing lookup at all.
- What read API does the directory expose for plan-time scans, and how does it avoid holding the ingest lock while a controller walks a salt?
- Which facts belong in the directory beyond placements — hit counts for LFU-style controllers, anything else a controller would otherwise store per key?
- What retention does the single topic need? It has to cover the longest expected coordinator downtime plus one snapshot interval, or a restart lands cold.
- What snapshot interval bounds catch-up acceptably, given catch-up replays every event since the checkpoint?
- Is it worth suppressing repeat `ACCESS` events at the producer, one touch per key per flush window, to keep the topic from being dominated by recency refreshes?
- Should the checkpoint be keyed by partition set from the start, so a future multi-replica coordinator does not invalidate every checkpoint on rebalance?
- Does `POST /directory/events` stay as an alias for one release, or is the rename to `POST /cache-events` a clean break?
- How much of this should be settled before the native port in #4065 starts, so the port copies the target shape rather than the current one?

## Expected outcome

Agreement on five things:

1. Ingest owns the stream: one gate fences, dedups, repairs gaps and holds the position, behind either an HTTP or an MQ source.
2. The key directory is the one per-key store, because the read APIs require it to exist anyway.
3. Controllers build their own state from the event stream, and no controller reads another.
4. Fold from the event, plan from the directory, and keep anything O(keys) in the directory.
5. Persistence is two components split by write trigger — a periodic checkpointer that records its stream position, and an on-change metadata persister.

Once that is agreed, the milestones above can land as small PRs in order.

items.title: fix(cacheblend): keep local matcher when fleet coordinator is enabled
items.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

### Problem
When a CacheBlend MP server is configured with a coordinator, `cb_unified_lookup` treated local fingerprint matching and fleet (coordinator) matching as **mutually exclusive**: the local matcher was skipped entirely and only fleet results were used.

That diverges from the documented contract in `docs/design/v1/mp_coordinator/blend_lookup.md` (**additive**: local always runs; coordinator only adds candidates). In practice it causes **false misses** when:

- cache-event flush to the coordinator is lagging,
- an event batch is dropped / token binding was evicted,
- the coordinator match deadline is exceeded (the code already logged “local-only”, but `job.matches` had been left empty).

### Motivation
Fleet index is best-effort, not a guaranteed superset of the local table. Running only fleet with a coordinator present makes recall strictly worse than local-only for the failure modes above. Additive union restores the intended robustness with only the cost of a local vectorized probe (already cheap on the path that pays for a coordinator RTT).

### Solution
1. Always run `_match_fingerprints` (emit `CB_FINGERPRINT_MATCH_*` as before).
2. After the prefix leg, poll the coordinator (unchanged defer/deadline behavior).
3. Build candidates with new `_union_match_candidates(local, fleet)` (local listed first so equal `cur_st` ties prefer local under the existing stable leftmost-greedy dedup).
4. Continue through `_non_overlapping_after_prefix` + sparse prefetch unchanged.
5. Docs: fix observability note that claimed the legs were mutually exclusive.

### Verification
Unit tests (pass):

```bash
pytest -q tests/v1/multiprocess/test_blend_v3_load_store_opts.py \
  -k 'union or fleet_timeout or coordinator_match'
# 7 passed
```

Also ran a local before/after recall check with the real `BlendTokenRangeMatcherV3` on `store=A+B+C`, `query=B+D+C` (fragment leg, `chunk_size=4`):

```text
### fleet_empty_event_lag
    local hits: 2  fleet hits: 0
    OLD (fleet-only w/ coord): 0 matches, 0 tokens
    NEW (local∪fleet):         2 matches, 8 tokens
    Δ tokens: +8  (IMPROVED)

### fleet_timeout
    OLD: 0 tokens → NEW: 8 tokens  (+8)

### fleet_partial_only_B
    OLD: 4 tokens → NEW: 8 tokens  (+4)

### fleet_complete_superset
    OLD: 8 tokens → NEW: 8 tokens  (+0, same)

### fleet_only_remote_chunk
    OLD: 4 tokens → NEW: 4 tokens  (+0, same)

SUMMARY: improved 3/5, unchanged 2/5, regressed 0/5
```

Steady-state (fleet already complete) and remote-only hits are unchanged; gains show up exactly when fleet is empty/partial/timed out while local still has content.

Note: full GPU vLLM + `lmcache_cacheblend` e2e was not run on this Mac (no CUDA / private plugin). The above validates the candidate-selection change this PR makes.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- Behavior change only when `_coordinator is not None`. No coordinator → same as before.
- Prefer local on `cur_st` ties intentionally (local L1 is more reliable for retrieve).
- Signed-off-by included (DCO).

- [x] this PR contains unit tests

labels.name: full

items.body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Refs #4226 (control-plane RFC). This is the emission half of the fleet-wide key directory (M1, directory side merged in #4275): MP servers stream `STORE`/`ACCESS`/`DELETE` cache events for **both tiers** to the coordinator's `/directory/events` — by riding the existing observability event bus rather than adding parallel listener plumbing.

- **One subscriber, no extra threads**: `CacheEventSubscriber` (on the `mp_observability` EventBus) maps the storage layer's key events onto the directory vocabulary, batches them order-preservingly (pending batches: consecutive same-identity entries coalesce, an identity change starts a new batch — a store→delete→re-store can never reorder), assigns per-instance `seq`, and delivers through `CacheEventSink` on the bus's drain thread. Flushing is interval-paced (`--coordinator-event-flush-interval`), with the L1 eviction loop's tick as the flush pump so burst-ending tails (e.g. L2 store completions) deliver promptly.
- **Transport seam**: the only sink today is HTTP push; a production message-queue sink (e.g. Kafka, partition key = `instance_id`) drops in without touching producers — the directory already absorbs at-least-once delivery (seq dedup), loss (gap detection → resync flag), and restarts (incarnation fencing, `incarnation` = server start time). Bus-queue overflow degrades the same way as transport loss.
- **Producers**: L1 store/evict events now carry `meta: list[L1ObjectMeta]` (per-object size + `L1Backend` medium via `L1ManagerProtocol.get_backend`; the Device-DAX tier resolves it per object through `MemoryObj.parent()`), so a hybrid DRAM+DAX L1 reports exactly where each object landed and deletes target the same placement identity. `touch_keys` publishes the new `l1.keys.accessed`. The L2 base adapter's notify funnel publishes `l2.keys.stored/accessed/deleted` with the adapter type name stamped at build time — **runtime-added adapters emit automatically**.
- `Tier` moves to `lmcache/v1/distributed/api.py` alongside the new `L1Backend` enum (`tiers.py` removed); `l1_primary_backend` lives next to `L1ManagerConfig`.

**User-facing changes**: `--coordinator-l2-event-reporting` / `--coordinator-l2-event-flush-interval` are replaced by `--coordinator-event-reporting` / `--coordinator-event-flush-interval` (env: `LMCACHE_COORDINATOR_EVENT_REPORTING` / `LMCACHE_COORDINATOR_EVENT_FLUSH_INTERVAL`). One flag gates both the key-directory stream and the existing quota stream (re-basing the quota stream onto this emitter is a follow-up PR). Event reporting requires observability enabled — combining it with `--disable-observability` fails fast at startup.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- Design doc: `docs/design/v1/mp_coordinator/cache_events.md` (transport contract, ordering/seq semantics, per-medium attribution, bus coupling); `docs/design/v1/mp_observability/event-bus.md` §7 updated for the third event category (loss-tolerant cache-event stream vs business-logic listeners vs observability).
- Verified end-to-end with vLLM (`LMCacheMPConnector`) + MP server + coordinator: directory placements matched on-disk L2 truth byte-for-byte (9/9 keys, L1+L2), ACCESS on prefix hit, DELETE removal across both tiers, and tick-driven tail delivery.
